{{Redirect|Lance Dixon|the baseball player|Lance Dickson}}
'''Lance Jenkins Dixon''' (born 22 June 1961, in [[Pasadena, California]]) is an American theoretical particle physicist. He is a professor in the [[SLAC Theory Group]] at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]] (SLAC) at [[Stanford University]].

Dixon received in 1982 his B.S. in physics and applied mathematics from [[Caltech]] and received in 1986 his doctorate from [[Princeton University]]. As a [[postdoc]] he was at SLAC. From 1987 he was assistant professor at Princeton University, from 1989 he was a Panofsky Fellow at the SLAC and in 1992 he became an associate professor and in 1998 a full professor at SLAC.

He has been a visiting professor at the [[École normale supérieure]] and the [[University of Cambridge]] ([[Clare Hall, Cambridge|Clare Hall]]).

In 1987, Dixon gave a talk at the [[International Centre for Theoretical Physics]] in [[Trieste]] where he described a symmetry of supersymmetric string theories that would become known as [[mirror symmetry]]. <ref>{{cite book |last=Dixon |first=Lance J.|date=1987 |editor-last= |editor-first= |title=Superstrings, unified theories, and cosmology, 1987 : proceedings of the Summer Workshop in High Energy Physics and Cosmology, Trieste, Italy, 29 June-7 August 1987 |publisher= |pages= |chapter=Some World-Sheet Properties of Superstring Compactifications, on Orbifolds and Otherwise |isbn=}}</ref>

Starting in the 1990s Dixon developed, with [[Zvi Bern]] and others, new methods (''generalized unitarity methods'' among others) for the calculation of [[Feynman diagram]]s in [[quantum chromodynamics]] (QCD) and other [[Yang–Mills theory|Yang–Mills theories]]. These new methods became more relevant with the requirements of the [[Large Hadron Collider]] calculations in the 2000s and also provided new insights into the divergences in the [[supergravity]] perturbation series.

In 2014, with [[Zvi Bern]] and [[David Kosower]], Dixon received the [[Sakurai Prize]] for "pathbreaking contributions to the calculation of perturbative scattering amplitudes, which led to a deeper understanding of quantum field theory and to powerful new tools for computing [[quantum chromodynamics|QCD]] processes."<ref>[http://www.aps.org/units/dpf/awards/recipient.cfm?first_nm=Lance&last_nm=Dixon&year=2014 Laudatio Sakurai Prize]</ref>

His 1991 publication<ref>{{cite journal|journal=Nuclear Physics B|volume=355|issue=3|date=27 May 1991|pages=649–688|title=Moduli dependence of string loop corrections to gauge coupling constants|author=Dixon, Lance J.|author2=Kaplunovsky, Vadim S.|author3=Louis, Jan|doi=10.1016/0550-3213(91)90490-O|bibcode=1991NuPhB.355..649D|osti=1449107 }}</ref> with Vadim S. Kaplunovsky and Jan Louis has over 800 citations. In 1995 Dixon was elected a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].

He was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2022.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2022-nas-election.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220503174757/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2022-nas-election.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=May 3, 2022 | title=2022 NAS Election }}</ref>
